sentences: On a snowy hilltop, we stand right behind the hunters, and below us a frozen valley and its village open out at a single glance.
Pieter Bruegel the Elder painted this winter scene in 1565, in oil on a wooden panel.
Three hunters trudge down the hill with their worn-out dogs.
Heads bowed, they press through the snow with heavy steps, and even the dogs look lean and weary.
In the snow, only a hare's tracks run past them.
Look at the back of the hunter on the left.
All they have to show for the day is one scrawny fox, so the hunt has mostly failed.
After a whole day out, they are coming home almost empty-handed.
Outside the inn on the left, villagers and a child have lit a fire to singe a pig.
Red flames and smoke whip sideways through the cold air, yet the hunters do not even turn to look.
Above them, the inn sign has half come away from its fittings and dangles precariously.
It names the house the Golden Hart and shows the vision of a stag seen by a patron saint of hunters.
Look up, and crows perch in the bare trees while a magpie glides across the sky.
Bruegel often painted such birds as ill omens.
Behind them, the winter sky is a cold, glassy green.
Bruegel sweeps the view diagonally down from the hunters' backs into a bird's-eye view of the whole valley.
It ends in jagged peaks that no flat Flemish landscape ever had, a world part real and part imagined.
Far below on the frozen ponds, tiny figures skate and play games much like curling.
With just a few dark silhouettes, Bruegel lets you almost hear their laughter and the scrape of blades on the ice.
At the lower right, the wheel of a watermill is frozen stiff, hung with icicles that tell us how harsh this winter is.
On the bridge beside it, a figure carefully passes with a bundle on their back.
The panel is thought to belong to a series of the seasons made for the Antwerp merchant Niclaes Jongelinck, and five of the six paintings survive.
The winter of 1565 is remembered as the start of a run of harsh winters.
It hangs today in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna.
It appears in the Russian director Tarkovsky's film Solaris, and the poet William Carlos Williams wrote a poem about it.
It holds a hard winter and the stubborn rhythm of everyday life in one frame.
Step back and ask yourself where your heart goes: to the weary hunters, or to the people at play below.
